maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MANION DISMISSAL OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY EMPLOYEES AT JOLIETTE

speechtext: On the orders of the day.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MANION DISMISSAL OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY EMPLOYEES AT JOLIETTE
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege. May I say that in some sixteen sessions this is, I think, the second time I have done so. It is in regard to a number of statements, all wrong, made by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Ferland) in a political
Privilege-Mr. Manion

speech delivered, I think, on July 1 in his constituency. For fear that I may be accused of mistranslating the hon. gentleman's remarks, I shall attempt in my halting way to read it first in French and then I shall read the translation, 'lire French version is as follows:
Le dernier orateur est M. C.-E. Ferland, depute au parlement federal. Apres avoir dit qu'il etait heureux de prendre part a cette assemblee, il parle du renvoi de 46 employes du C.N..R. "Je veux dire", dit-il, "aux ouvriers affectes par cette decision funeste du gouverne-ment conservateur de jeter sur le pave qua-rante six employes, toils pores de famille-plu-sieurs d'entre eux avaient droit a un fonds de pension-qu'il y a la une injustice considerable."
"Des le renvoi de ces citoyens, on m'a notifie au moyen d'un telegramme. Je me suis occupe de cette affaire immediatement et je regrette aujourd'hui de dire que je blame le ministre des Chemins de fer, l'honorable Dr R. J. Manion parce qu'il a refuse de recevoir une delegation d'ouvriers de Joliette qui voulaient aller le rencontrer a ce sujet. Une lettre dans mon bureau a Ottawa atteste ce que j'avance.
"Je suis content ee soir de rencontrer les ouvriers du C.N.R. et les autres pour les mettre au courant de ce refus du ministre eonserva-teur."
This is the translation:
The last speaker is Mr. C. E. Ferland, federal member. After saying that he was glad to take part in this meeting, he spoke of the dismissal of forty-six Canadian National Railway employees. "I wish to say," he said, "to the labourers affected by this disastrous decision of the Conservative government, throwing forty-six employees on the pavement-
I suppose that means the street.

all fathers of families-a few of them entitled to a pension-that there is a terrible injustice."
That is the first statement that is not correct, because the federal government has nothing whatever to do with the laying off of employees by the Canadian National Railways. The management of the railways handle entirely the matter of employment, the maintenance of the road and work such as that without consultation in any shape or form with the government of Canada. Then the hon. member says:
I was notified by telegram as soon as these employees were dismissed. I took the matter in hand immediately and regret to say that I blame the Minister of Railways, the Hon. Doctor R. J. Manion, because he refused to receive a delegation of the labourers of Joliette, who wanted to meet him in this connection. A letter in my office in Ottawa confirms this statement.
I am glad to meet to-night the Canadian National Railways employees and to let them know the refusal of the Conservative minister.
He says that I refused to receive a delegation of the labourers of Joliette. I was never

asked either by the hon. member for Joliette or anybody else, to meet a delegation so I could not very well refuse. Secondly, he says that a letter in his office in Ottawa confirms his statement. That, of course, is just as far from the facts as the other statement was, I am going to read his letter to me and the house will see whether he asked me to receive a deputation. I shall read my reply to him and then I shall make one comment. This was written by my hon. friend on House of Commons paper under date of June 26:
Dear Mr. Manion:
You will please find enclosed a telegram which I received this morning from Mr. Hector Mainville of Joliette, regarding the Canadian National Railway's decision to lay off forty men out of sixty men now employed in ear department at Joliette, Quebec.
This shows that my hon. friend knew as well as I do it was the management of the railways that laid off the men. The letter continues:
May I venture to say that the above decision is in violation of the terms of an existing contract which obliges the Canadian National Railways to maintain in permanence at Joliette (one of its divisional points), not less than fifty men in that car department, according to the interpretation of Canadian National Railway officials.
I wish you would kindly investigate and see that no unlawful act or injustice is done.
With my best regards, I remain, sir,
Yours truly,
Charles E. Ferland.
He did not ask me to meet a deputation of any kind. I replied acknowledging that letter, and I will read my letter in a moment. He accompanied this letter with a telegram which had been sent to him by Hector Mainville, from Joliette, reading as follows;
Charles E. Ferland, M.P.,
Ottawa.	.
Officially decided by Canadian National officials that effective July first forty men out of sixty will be laid off in car department whereas at other points in this district reduction only amounts from ten to twenty per cent. Conditions most disastrous and delegation wants to meet you at your office soon as possible.	_
Hector Mainville.
In other words, they asked to meet Mr. Ferland. Mr. Ferland sends me a copy of this telegram, which speaks of a delegation wanting to meet him. My reply to Mr. Ferland was as follows:
Ottawa, June 29, 1931.
Dear Mr. Ferland,-
I have received your communication of the 26th instant, and will pass it on to the railway management for their consideration, as the matter is one entirely in the hands of the

Quebec Leader of Opposition
officials. You will, therefore, appreciate that the deputation should see the management and that there would really be no use in their coming to Ottawa.
To see Mr. Ferland, as the telegram said. I was not asked to meet any deputation. The ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) smiles, but so far as my statement is concerned, it is absolutely in accordance with the facts. I was not asked to see a deputation. Mr. Mainville asked to see Mr. Ferland, with a deputation and I told them that the best thing to do was to see the management. To show my good faith in the matter, I might mention that I wrote to Sir Henry Thornton, enclosing Mr. Ferland's protest and a copy of the telegram. I have brought this matter up, Mr. Speaker, because the hon. gentleman has been in the habit-this is not the first time-of making such mis-statements. I think there is decency and honesty in public life that should be respected even by that hon. gentleman.

I have a little amendment here, which I am quite sure you will not rule out of order, Mr. Chairman. Might I take

the time of the committee for one minute to make a suggestion that I hope will expedite business-and goodness knows that is a praiseworthy ambition.
I want to congratulate you, sir, on the way you handled the points of order which were raised. You allowed the hon. member to state his point of order and the other hon. member concerned to state his conception of the matter. Then you invited any other hon. member who wished to say anything in connection with the point of order to state his views before giving your decision. I consider that to be the ideal practice; if it had been followed at all times during this session we would not have had the very large number of appeals we have had from rulings of the chairman. The chairman is inviting a member to appeal to the house when he says, "You are out of order. Sit down! If you do not like it you can appeal." In this case there was an appeal taken, but if your practice were followed it would leave hon. members with the feeling that they had been given a fair run for their money and a chance to state their point before the matter was decided.
I say if that had been done by the Speaker and Deputy Speaker there would not have been the very numerous appeals which have been made this session.
After that piece of flattery, Mr. Chairman,
I am quite sure you will not find fault with the amendment I am going to suggest, and in any case it is so appropriate that it cannot fail to bring with it its own welcome. I propose to insert after the word "aforesaid" in line 26 of subsection 2 the words "or examine witnesses". If the amendment is adopted the section then will read:
The board shall give reasonable opportunity to persons who may not have been summoned, to appear before them and give evidence upon oath or solemn affirmation as aforesaid, or examine witnesses, on any matter relevant to an inquiry then being held by the board.
The right hon. Prime Minister was courteous enough, and I think showed sound judgment in doing so, to accept an amendment to the effect that these hearings should be held in what is called open court, and the amendment I propose is so absolutely ancillary to that and so dependent upon it that it follows as a natural consequence that this amendment should be accepted also.
We have this situation: We have a court of record, which, in my layman's ignorance, I understand ranks at least with a county court, if no higher. We are to have public hearings, in accordance with the usual court practice. We are to have witnesses called to give evidence under oath, and then sud-

Tariff Board
fdenly this procedure departs from that ladopted in the ordinary court of record; there is no provision made for examining the *witnesses. Can you conceive a man taking *a case into court with the understanding that this witnesses shall not be examined? It may Ibe said that this is different from an ordinary Icourt, but these commissioners have been lalluded to as exercising judicial functions and as being in the position of judges, and I *accept that statement. Then surely the judges icannot cross-examine the witnesses; that Svould show partiality or bias to one side or *the other. To use the language of the courts, we might say there is in court a plaintiff directly or indirectly seeking the endorsation of the tariff board in connection with his proposed tariff increase. The plaintiff is heard *under oath; the witnesses for the plaintiff *can be heard, but the defendant in the case, the unhappy public, the consumer who must pay the piper in the long run, is not to be heard at all. There is provision that he may come in and give evidence but he cannot cross-examine the other witnesses, which is the vital point.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if this amendment is not accepted we might as well tear up the whole bill, because this will be only a one-sided court at the most. The pressure of public opinion is a very great thing, and if we are to have no publicity nine-tenths of the usefulness of this court will disappear. There will be no protection for the ordinary man in the street, to whom we refer so often as the consumer. We might as well go back to the old system, under which the representatives of the manufacturing interests met the minister in his office and told him any sort of story they wished to tell, leaving the minister to find out the truth as best he could. If we are not to have this provision in this bill we might as well let the minister continue as he has gone on in the past, aided perhaps by a committee of the cabinet and one or two technical men to get information on detailed points.
Why should there not be opportunity to examine witnesses? What objection can there be to this suggestion? If a man has a good case, I care not what court he is before, whether it is this parliament, the tariff board or some other court, he is not ashamed of anything he might be asked; he is anxious to present the whole truth and nothing but the truth to the men who are acting as judges or jurors. Take the case of two men charged with a major crime, say that of murder. The innocent man is only too willing to talk about his case to every person who will listen to
him. He is not afraid to answer quickly because he knows he is telling the truth and he cannot be tripped up in connection with some previous answer. He is willing to go into the witness box himself, although it is not to his discredit if he does not do so. He is willing to tell all he knows, to tell it to everybody and at length. On the other hand, the man who knows he is guilty is not going into the witness box unless he cannot help it, and if he does give evidence he will be very careful of his answers. He will say to himself, "If I say this it may conflict with what I said before; I must be careful. I would rather not go into the witness box, and above all I would rather not be cross-examined." The innocent man knows he has a good case and is quite willing to tell his story and be cross-examined upon it, because he knows that the more he gets his facts before the court the better will be his chances of success.
I might quote one instance; I need not go into details, because I think I have already mentioned it in the house. A certain duly incorporated manufacturing company, which I believe was really more of a private company, came to the tariff board asking for an increase of tariff in connection with a certain product. I think the president, or vice-president, the accountant and one or two lawyers appeared to present the case of the company. I happened to be present; it concerned a product used by dairymen, and I took some interest in the application. The beginning, the end and a great deal of the middle of the argument of each gentleman was that the company had been in business so many years and had lost money consistently during the previous seven or eight years because of the lack of a proper tariff. That was the burden of their song; whenever they got stuck in some other argument they fell back on the statement that they were losing heavily and could not make both ends meet; they saw ruin, destitution and starvation before them because of the lack of the tariff they requested.
This went on for so long, and the argument was reiterated so often that at last it dawned even on my slow-acting intelligence that "the lady doth protest too much," and I asked to be allowed to secure from thie gentlemen who were giving this evidence a copy of the 'balance sheet of the company for the last four or five years, in order to demonstrate just how much they had been losing and to see whether or not it was cumulative, because that was their argument. They said they lost so much in 1924 and so much in 1925 and the loss was getting bigger all the time. Remember, this was an incorporated company.
Tariff Board

but the president said, "No, not on your life; I did not come down here to spread my balance sheets before all and sundry." But my request was upheld, and he was ordered to produce his balance sheets within the next thirty days, or before the next hearing. Some very trivial excuse was made as to why the sheets were not presented at the next hearing, and again I was given permission to get them before the following hearing, but before that time came I was informed that the gentleman had thrown up his hands and would rather be without any more tariff protection than produce his books, which would have conclusively proved his own case if his argument had been sound. I will admit that he was not under oath, but surely that was only a detail. How would the board have obtained information on which to give a fair and equitable decision if they were not furnished with those balance sheets, and how would they have obtained them if I or someone else had not been there to ask that they be produced? That is a fair although trivial! illustration of the need of someone being allowed to go there and ask a few simple questions.

I have put the case in the best way I can. Recently the Prime Minister emphasized and reiterated at some length the fact that this legislation is motivated by a sincere desire to constitute a board which will be in the best interests of the manufacturer, the workman and the consumer. Up to the present moment I have been inclined to accept that view although it may have needed a little stretching of that imagination to which the Secretary of State dbjeets. I am willing to concede that up to this point the Prime Minister has been sincere and the legislation may do what he says it is intended to do, but should this amendment not be allowed I must change my viewpoint because I could not then see how it could be sincere or how it- could be successful. It would be one-way justice; the scales of justice will be loaded down against the consumer and in favour of the man making the application. A man may be applying for an increased tariff or for a reduced tariff, but there is an opposite side to any tariff application. The man on the opposite side should be given an opportunity 
to examine the witnesses who appear and swear, so to speak, against him, or at least in opposition to his own views. I earnestly urge the Prime Minister to consider the acceptance of this very small amendment.
