Tariff Board
Everyone is not to be allowed to jump up on the back seats and ask a question, there must be some measure of decorum observed in the conduct of the business of the tribunal. The provision in that regard is that the board shall make the rules for the conduct of its affairs. I have no doubt that those who may be interested will be given the fullest opportunity to cross-examine or deal with these matters, but that must be done under the regulations of the court itself. In respect to the inquiry which is now being held in this building it was determined in the first instance who were the interested parties, whether or not they should be represented by counsel, and otherwise. This subsection provides that the first duty of the board will be to make rules with respect to these matters and to prevent someone jumping up and saying he is going to ask a question of the witness. The first procedure is to know who are the appearances, to use the language of courts, who is to appear for the different parties. This amendment of the hon. gentleman deals solely with the question of witnesses and would have the effect of introducing a practice which cannot be accepted in any sense as having any relevancy to that particular section.
I acknowledge that the government has the power to defeat this amendment if it chooses to do so, but I would prefer to see it voted down rather than to be sidetracked by the use of a point of order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not raising a question beyond saying that it is not-

The right hon. gentleman has suggested that I might find my remedy or recourse under subsection 12, but it would take an imagination beyond that which I possess to see in that subsection any provision of this character. The subsection reads:
The board shall hold its sessions and conduct its proceedings in such manner as may seem to it most convenient for the speedy and efficient discharge of its duties.
The board might decide that the hearing of witnesses without their being cross-examined would lend itself to the speedy discharge of its duties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: "Speedy and efficient" are the words.

There is a difference of opinion as to the meaning of the word " efficient", and that difference might apply in view of the pre-supposed opinions of the
members of the board with regard to tariff matters. I remember a few years ago when sitting on the opposite side of the chamber that a matter somewhat similar to this came up on a bill in connection with soldier settlement. I rose in my place and asked the minister in charge of the bill if it meant such-and-so. I wanted an amendment included to express my ideas, but the minister replied that it was not necessary, that it certainly meant such-and-so. Six months afterwards the department wrote me and totally disavowed the Iviews to which expression had been given in the house, and said that they were bound by the letter of the statute. Of course it was open to me to say that I remembered it to be such-and-so and give my own conception of what was meant by the statute but that did not prevail. However, going back to the word "witnesses" I really think the Prime Minister has a misconception of where this amendment should be included in the bill. He states that I am giving the power to witnesses to appear and to cross-examine other witnesses. Subsection 1 reads:
The board shall have the power of summoning before them any witnesses, and of requiring them to give evidence on oath ....
Subsection 2, to which I have been referring, reads:
The board shall give reasonable opportunity to persons who may not have been summoned, to appear before them

	*

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Who may not have been Isummoned; it refers only to witnesses because they are the only ones who can be summoned.
It applies to people who have not been summoned. You summon witnesses but you do not summon everyone else. That is my point. It applies to people who have not been summoned to appear before them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And to give evidence.

Not necessarily. The subsection reads:
The board shall give reasonable opportunity to persons who may not have been summoned,-
Who are not going to be witnesses at the request of the court-
-to appear before them.
The subsection grants only one thing, the privilege to appear and give evidence under oath, but I am asking for the privilege of lappearing at the inquiry to examine witnesses. A man has the power to give evidence, but I want him to be given the opportunity of cross-examining his opposing witnesses, so to speak. This is very important as far as the
Tariff Board

consumer is concerned. With all due deference to the legal acumen of my right hon. friend, and allowing for my ignorance in the matter, I submit the point of order is not well taken.
The question is on the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime
Minister complained yesterday that we on this side of the chamber did not appear to be able to understand the obvious meaning of words. After listening to this debate for the last few days, I confess that I am in the dark as to exactly how proceedings will be carried on before this board. In order that the committee may have a clear understanding of this procedure, I would like to state to the Prime Minister a specific case and have him tell us exactly what would happen. Let us suppose that a manufacturer of steel plates makes an application to the minister for higher duties. The application will be accompanied by a brief in which they will set forth the reasons why they consider their application should be granted. They will state their investment, overhead, cost of raw material, wage costs, market conditions quantity of their product, quantity of imports and everything else that they conceive has any bearing on the question. The minister then, if I understand the matter aright, will submit that brief to the board and he will say to it: Get us all the facts in connection with the matter. The board will make an investigation and will report whether the facts as it finds them as outlined in the brief are correct or not as the case may be.
But there is another set of facts that should have a bearing on the case in so far as the government's decision is concerned, and that is how this decision, if rendered, will affect the consuming public. Those steel sheets that were mentioned are the raw material of the stove makers, the makers of kitchen utensils, of filing cabinets, of a hundred and one other things. Any change in the tariff consequent upon the advice given by the board in this matter will therefore affect the production costs of these other manufacturers. I want to ask the minister whether these other manufacturers, so affected, will be given notice that this case is coming up and an opportunity to appear either personally or by counsel; whether that counsel or whoever they send to represent them will be permitted to give evidence as to how this decision will affect their business, and also to examine the witnesses of those who are making the appli-

cation. If the minister will answer that question specifically, perhaps I shall be able to understand how the board is going to proceed in such cases.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: First, let us assume that the application is made and referred to the board with the relevant papers. Second, the board will be convened at a date to be named for the purpose of hearing the application. Third, witnesses such as might be required would be summoned, if necessary by subpoena, and directed, if necessary, to bring their papers-in other words, as we lawyers say, subpoena duces tecum. Fourth, reasonable opportunity will be given to persons not summoned, to appear and give evidence under oath. Five, the board would otherwise, I take it, in the conduct of the inquiry, comply with its rules and regulations as it promulgated them under the provisions of subsection 12 of section 5. At the opening of the inquiry, as I would expect it would be conducted, it would call for the appearances, and as the hon. gentleman said, if counsel appeared for the stove makers, in my judgment he would have an opportunity >to crossexamine the witnesses that had appeared and given evidence in the earlier part of the inquiry as it proceeded. I can conceive of no rules being made that would not make some provision for that, and if hon. gentlemen believe they would feel easier in their minds if the government were charged with the responsibility, they may add to subsection 12 that the rules and regulations promulgated by the board shall be published in the Canada Gazette, so that there may be no question in regard to that.

If anybody appears voluntarily, will the board have power under subsection 2 to refuse to listen to their evidence? To take as an example the case mentioned by the hon. member for Weyburn, if counsel representing the stove makers appears, will the board have power to refuse to listen to his representations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
confusing the question of representation made by counsel and evidence presented by witnesses. His first question was whether the board would have power to refuse to hear a witness that appeared. In my judgment, if a witness appeared and said: "I am here to give evidence in this inquiry," this is made to meet that very case. If counsel undertook to make statements without evidence, I assume the court would treat counsel exactly

Tariff Board
as a court of record would do and say: Mr. So-and-so, please confine yourself to the evidence in the record. The hon. gentleman is familiar with the practice of courts in that regard.

I am not quite clear yet in regard to my question. If the stove makers in this case send a man to represent them before the board, will he be permitted to fulfil the dual function of giving evidence and examining witnesses?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The courts have universally held that except in very rare cases no man should be both witness and counsel. The reason is obvious, for the summing up involves the necessity of his referring to his own testimony. That has been wholly frowned upon by the courts of the country. I recall one case in which the court permitted counsel to go into the box and prove a fact that had to be proven merely as a formal matter, but where evidence touching the merits of a controversy is concerned, our courts have universally held that as a matter of sound practice and regard for the amenities between the court and members of the bar, no person should be witness and counsel at the same time. The case was very fully discussed on one occasion by the courts of the country. In a case before the Supreme Court of Canada on appeal from one of the provinces, counsel gave evidence as a witness, and was compelled during the argument to refer to the witness so-and-so and so-and-so. The court said that this was very unsound practice and I think practically no member of the profession in these days would suggest that it be followed.
Would the converse be true, that a man could appear and represent any particular interest without giving evidence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is what I conceive
will be covered by the rules and regulations governing the court. If it be thought desirable that rules so promulgated should be approved by the governor in. council and appear in the Canada Gazette, I am wholly willing that an amendment to that effect be added.

When the Prime Minister
speaks of representation by counsel, I should like to ask him whether representation is to be by counsel only or whether an agent could fulfil the duties. My experience in connection with the old tariff board was that frequently lawyers appeared before it whose understanding of the problems which were being inquired into was not as profound as that of laymen.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My conception of the
duty of any court is when opening the inquiry and calling for appearances, to note the representatives that are present. It need not be a professional man who represents the parties my hon. friend has mentioned.
Thanks for that much.
I thank the Prime Minister very much for his assurance. If he agrees with that, why not put it in the bill and make us happy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Because I have seen it
abused; that is the reason. I do think there must be some measure of decorum in the conducting of matters of this kind. It is wholly beside the question to have someone appear and claim the right to cross-examine and then to make statements, not under oath, which are not statements of fact, but which they ask to be accepted as facts.
Amendment (Mr. Neill) negatived, on division.
Subsections 3 to 6 inclusive, of section 5, agreed to.
On section 5, subsection 7-Powers of one member.

I should like
to make it clear that one of the powers conferred upon the board is to determine what increases of duty are to be made in certain cases.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

I was abbreviating. Section 4 says:
Ip respect of goods produced in or imported into Canada the board shall, under the direction of the minister, make inquiry as to-
(b) the cost of production in Canada and elsewhere, and what increases or decreases in rates of duty are required to equalize differences in the cost of production.
I was assuming that the finding of the board with respect to what increases of duty were required would involve the drawing of an inference upon which the government would act. The point I wish to make clear is that one member of the board alone, under the subsection that we are now considering, will have all the power's that in section 4 are conferred upon the board. In other words, the government may be advised on these matters by just one member of the board who may take the investigation in hand. It is not a full board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On more than one
occasion it has been found desirable, in a country as large as this, that there should be
Tariff Board

on the part of every member of a given tribunal the power to make inquiries. This subsection enables that power to be exercised by one member-the next subsection provides for two members having power to conduct inquiries in certain matters-the evidence being taken by one member of the board and not by all.

I understand
the reason, that it-may be desired to spread the members around a bit. But it comes down to this, that one individual exercises all the powers of this board for the purpose of the inquiry to be made under section 4.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
For the purpose of the
inquiry, but not for the purpose of the report.

The report
is signed just as a matter of course.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, they may agree or
disagree. The report is by the full board.
Subsection 7 agreed to.
Subsection 8 agreed to.
On section 5, subsection 9.-Power to proceed on other than sworn evidence.

I think this is an extraordinary section. It simply means that members of the board may make a finding on anything they pick up anywhere in any way. That goes very far for a court. I have never heard of a court being able to pronounce judgment on information that it has gathered in the highways and by-ways, but that is exactly what is being done here. It says:
For the purposes of any inquiry under this act, the board may obtain information, which in their judgment is authentic-
They have only to believe it is authentic.
-otherwise than under the sanction of an oath or affirmation, and use and act upon such information.
All they have to do is to believe the information is authentic, and then they may use or act upon such information. With this subsection in the bill what is the good of the other subsections of section 5, which provide that evidence shall be taken under oath?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Supreme Court of Canada, in the case of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company vs. McKinnon, a gentleman of the legal profession, decided that it was competent for a board of arbitrators to arrive at a conclusion of their own knowledge. Rightly or wrongly, the general rule has been that you must have regard,

shall I say, to the common sense of individuals, and their sense of integrity and obligation. I have seen it happen that judges sometimes view the locus in quo for the purpose of ascertaining just how a machine may operate. They may hear the evidence with relation to it, and very often their own knowledge amplifies the evidence given. So that these words have acquired at least a general meaning. The League of Nations carries on very extensive inquiries, as I mentioned this afternoon. Evidence might be introduced with respect to that, but it is predicated upon the assumption that the board believes the information to be authentic. I recall thinking as the right hon. gentleman did, when that case went to the Supreme Court of Canada on appeal from the Supreme Court of Alberta. It did look a -bit strange that after admitting that the evidence was very contradictory the arbitrators should of their own knowledge arrive at the conclusion that the land was worth so much. Mr. McKinnon appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada. Any student of the law will 'be able to find the judgment. The case was over fifteen years ago. I realize that this subsection is a broad one, but it is the only one that would authorize reputable men charged with a sense of their own responsibility and regard for their oath of office, and who cannot at all times secure evidence under oath with respect to matters of this kind, to act upon information which they believe to be authentic and to which full credence should be given.
My right hon. friend has cited the Calgary case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Calgary and Edmonton Railway.
I think he knows himself that it has not very much to do with what we are discussing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It has everything to do with it.

I submit that it has not, as I shall show. My right horn friend is talking of a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, that arbitrator's might act of their own knowledge. The point made here is that this board, which is a court of record and has power to compel the attendance of witnesses and to pay their fees, is not obliged to do that but may obtain from any source information which they believe to be authentic. They may ask somebody in the street, or take information from newspaper articles

Tariff Board
or reports, so long as they believe it is authentic. I submit to my right hon. friend that is far from deciding that men may act on their own judgment, because every day the courts take judicial notice of matters within the knowledge of ordinary men. There are many matters in connection with which a complete knowledge of the facts and circumstances makes the taking of evidence unnecessary. That, however, is not what this section is for. It is not to authorize the board to act on their own knowledge; they have that power anyway. It authorizes them to act on the knowledge of somebody else without the solemnity of a oath. If the board so desires it has the right to issue subpoenas for the witnesses they wish to call. 1 am sure my right hon. friend has not given the true reason for this subsection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I object to that statement, because I have given the true reason with respect to it.

I submit to my right hon. friend that if the subsection is placed in the bill for the purpose of allowing the board to exercise their own knowledge there is no need for it, because the Calgary case decides that such bodies may use their own knowledge. If on the other hand the board is to be enabled to obtain information elsewhere, then I submit such action would not be within the four corners of court procedure, with which my right hon. friend is so familiar. The subsection is entirely unnecessary, because through the powers given to the board by my right hon. friend, any man can be forced to come before the board, if it so wills, and give evidence with the solemnity of an oath. Why have a seal? Why have the board constituted as a board of record? Why have power to summon witnesses? Why have power to imprison? W'hy have all these powers if one member of the court may ask his friend, whom he regards as entirely reliable, a particular question and act on the information he receives in reply thereto?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But it would have to be reported to parliament.

I understand that. That is what this section does; unless the information is of a confidential character it has to be reported to parliament-and I shall deal with that feature in a moment. I submit that the section is entirely unnecessary if its purpose is to enable the board to act on their own knowledge. It is entirely foreign to the
whole spirit of procedure, the functions and fundamentals of the tribunal, if it is for the purpose of enabling the board to act on information other than that taken under oath.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have given my hon. friend an illustration, namely information required with respect to a foreign government. A communication is despatched to the proper officer and a reply is received. This section enables such a reply to be used because it is believed that such information is true, without the solemnity of an oath. Such provision is absolutely essential in the conduct of inquiries, and there has been a custom-not in courts, but in other bodies-to rely upon the authenticity of information supplied by the public departments of the government of Great Britain. Not every day, but frequently, we act upon information received from public departments in Great Britain and the other dominions. This information is not given under oath but is believed to be reliable and is acted upon. It will be observed that in section 6 there is provision that a copy of any evidence taken, and information obtained, except it be of a confidential nature, shall be laid before parliament by the minister. So it is incumbent upon the board to make a record of the information obtained. It will be observed in the reports of the tariff commission of the United States to which I directed attention that in two instances they gave illustrations of information thus obtained. This is to meet that situation.
If the provision is only to meet the situation of getting information from a 'foreign government, my right hon. friend should say so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There are other cases.

He should not make the section world wide in character in order to get certain official information. As he knows, evidence of the actions of foreign governments and all official actions are taken judicial notice of by the courts through the solemnity of a seal and the certificate of a proper officer. I am sure he does not need this section for that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This section goes beyond that.

I suppose but for this section it would be necessaiy for the tariff board to bring before them the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of National Revenue to take an oath every time the board referred to annual statistics.
Tariff Board

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That might be so. My hon. friend has given what seems to be a very clear illustration.

May I point out that under this section the board may conduct its whole inquiry, make its report and act upon the information it secures, without taking any evidence under oath at all. Leaving out the words "otherwise than under the sanction of an oath or affirmation" the section would read:
For the purposes of any inquiry under this act, the board may obtain information which in their judgment is authentic, and use and act upon such information.
That is all they need to do. Whoever is in charge may secure and act upon whatever information he wishes so long as he believes such information to be authentic.
Does the right hon. gentleman seriously suggest any court would do that?
Whether any court would do it?

Yes, would any court do
that?

It is an utter absurdity to assume that economic phenomena can be dealt with in the same manner as that in which legal phenomena or questions of property and civil rights can be dealt with. It would be much better to simplify the terms of the bill by providing that the minister may obtain such information as he desires from any source in which he has confidence. That would be a guide to the minister. When he comes before parliament he has to take responsibility with respect to his presentations to parliament, and to my mind if that course were adopted the matter would be dealt with in a straightforward way. To go to the trouble to pass an act of parliament creating a court with all kinds of powers, dignities and the like, and insert in the bill a provision that the court may ignore all the powers so conferred upon it and act upon information it picks up on the highways and by-ways, seems' to me to be ridiculous.

Some people have complained that there are too many oaths in courts of law'. Subsection 1 of section 5 states that evidence may be given on oath or on solemn affirmation. I believe the experience of lawyers is that they have enough trouble to get the truth when witnesses are under oath. I doubt whether the truth could be had at all if witnesses gave evidence only on

solemn affirmation. I do not see how an inquiry could be conducted seriously by asking questions of witnesses who are only on solemn affirmation and not on oath.

I should like to ask
the Prime Minister whether a case such as I shall outline would come under the provisions of subsection 9 and 10, which impose secrecy concerning confidential information. Assume the board has written to or requested the head of some firm to give a statement. The head of that firm has supplied the board with a letter or document containing certain trade secrets, and in asking for an increased tariff the firm has used arguments based upon such trade secrets. Could the board then take action based upon such a letter or document, which in its nature was confidential and could not be brought down before parliament, and of which no parties save the board and the interested manufacturer could possibly be cognizant? It seems to me that a provision which would permit of such a case would be very wide indeed. The conditions I have outlined are not at all inconceivable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are possible.

The Prime Minister says they are possible-I would say that in many case they are probable. Under this section the board may bring before it the president of a company, And if the president of a company does not wish to be placed on oath so that the examination can run all along the line with regard to any questions that may be asked, the board under this section can simply get such information from him as they desire and then act upon it. Under the next subsection they may take his evidence in secret and may act upon it. I said the other day that this court is a star chamber foody, and I think that is amply borne out by these tw*o sections. It can if it suits its purposes put certain persons under oath, but other persons it may exempt from testifying under oath, it may use such evidence and conduct its business in secret and act upon the information obtained in that way. I do not believe there was a court in the reign of Charles I that ever had wider powers than that.
That is Tory policy.

The case that I mentioned is not merely a- hypothetical case, it is one that is exceedingly probable, and I think it is such a case as should, if possible, be guarded against.
Subsection 9 carried on division.

Tariff Board
On section 5, subsection 10-Confidential evidence or information not to be (made public.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
At the foot of the last line will be observed the words:
-to a penalty not exceeding $1,000 or to twelve months' imprisonment.
It is thought that the words "not more than" should be inserted before the words "to twelve months' imprisonment."

In that connection, Mr. Chairman, I should have added when speaking about this star chamber court that in addition to all that I have said1, it has the power of fine and imprisonment. I think that is a perfectly ludicrous power to give to any court dealing with questions of this kind. Why do we need, with respect to questions [DOT] affecting prices, powers of fine and imprisonment, especially where the body is an advisor}' body? I think it is going altogether too far so to trespass on the rights of the people in matters that affect their everyday lives-the prices at which they are to sell their commodities, the rates they are to get for wages, the cost of their living, taxation-all these things are involved, and the star chamber court is to have the right to fine and imprison persons from whom they think they are not getting all the information they ought to get and in the way they think they ought to get it. It seems to me it would be better to cut out fine and imprisonment and let the Prime Minister create a court that shall have power to investigate only. Let him go easy on the penalties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This court has no such power. I am amazed that the right hon. gentleman should not at least do himself the credit of reading the words in this subsection.
I have read the subsection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why did he endeavour to mislead the committee? This court has no such power to fine or imprison.
Has not a court of record power to fine and imprison?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not on summary conviction.

I am not talking about
summary conviction. The test of a court of record is whether it has power to fine or imprison.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It has power to enforce
law and order in the conduct of its proceedings.
Yes, and punish for contempt, which is by fine and imprisonment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It may do either. But
that is not the point. The hon. gentleman did not make that point.
I did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth is taking his usual course. He is endeavouring now to squirm out of something that somebody else has done instead of meeting the issue squarely. As I said, the right hon. leader of the opposition has not taken the trouble to read the subsection, because had he done so he would find that no such power is conferred.

I have read it
fifty times.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The power of summary
conviction is the power conferred upon magistrates under the criminal code, and when the right hon. gentleman suggests that this power should not be given, the extreme case that was put by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) is itself some indication of the reason why. If trade secrets are to be given away, if a man's business is to be destroyed, it is hardly to be expected that there should not be some punishment given to the person who did it. I rather think the right hon. gentleman on mature consideration will acknowledge that his use of the words "star chamber" is hardly warranted, for this reason; that he himself and some of his friends suggest that this should be a public inquiry, and we have agreed that it should be so.
Subject to the further clauses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Subject to the confidential clauses. But in a broad and general way a court that is a public court can hardly be termed a star chamber court-not very well. It was not the public quality of the star chamber which won for it that name. This is no more a star chamber court than the advisory tariff board was a star chamber court. Why is it there is such feeling about this legislation? One denunciation is that it is ridiculous. Well, if it is ridiculous, the responsibility rests with us. If it is useless, then why spend two or three days in opposing it? If it is harmless-as it is said to be-then why take all this time trying to prove that it is harmless? Time will demonstrate whether it is harmless or not. I have been very frank with the committee. I concede that very large powers are conferred, because very large responsibilities are being accepted, and very

Tariff Board

large efforts towards a given end are being made. Every now and then I hear hon. gentlemen opposite say there is some sinister meaning behind this, and they ask what is meant by it. I can only say to the committee that this means exactly what it says. When the right hon. gentleman suggests, why don't we pass a few sections and say that is the end of it, I ask why did Australia elaborate its position?
My right hon. friend is not following Australia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But why did Australia
elaborate its position?
Because it was a question as to whether it should be voluntary or compulsory.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In India a statute was
passed with respect to one commodity, namely, steel, and 'the tariff was fixed for a given time. The evidence was published. I read it in England-I do not know whether I brought it with me-and I have no doubt the right hon. leader of the opposition is familiar with it. It is a most illuminating volume as to the methods pursued for ascertaining the facts. However great the difference may be between us with respect to this, cannot we realize that there is no sinister object behind this legislation? This bill represents a very great deal of toil, the perusal of many statutes, and an honest endeavour to secure an enactment that would at least represent the good qualities and virtues of all existing legislation, and eliminate, that which was evil and useless. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that this will not work successfully. It may not, but if it does not it will not be because we have not tried to make it so. I have had strong convictions on this matter for longer years than I care to think of as I look back upon them, and having the opportunity I have endeavoured to crystallize those convictions into legislation, not as perfect as I should like it to be because of the pressure of time, but it represents an earnest effort to pass a statute whose operations will protect alike the consumer and the producer on the one hand, and on the other the public in the larger sense as representing the state itself. That is what we are trying to do. Why cannot we discuss the bill in that sense?

May I say to my- right hon. friend that I do not think I would be as suspicious of the legislation as I am or have the feeling about it that I have if it contained a provision that the parties themselves might appear before the court,

make application t.o be heard and have any question inquired into that they wished. But that is not the bill before us. This is legislation which will give my right hon. friend alone power to say what is to go before the court. He says he has been thinking over this matter for a long time-I believe he is right. He says he wants to give protection to the manufacturer, to the consumer and to labour-I believe that is true. But let me say this to him. These people are all able to protect themselves if you give them a chance; I do not think we need a new protector in this country. I do not think the interests of manufacturers, of labour and of consumers should be only under the guardianship of my right hon. friend, no matter how sincere he may be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not quite fair.

That is fair,
because my right hon. friend knows, and has laid it down to-day as a principle, that all the investigations under this act depend in the first instance upon his say-so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so, within the limits of the act itself.

My right hon. friend admits it, and that being the case I say I am frankly suspicious as to the good the measure will accomplish. If it were a measure freely conferring powers upon individuals to appear and be heard when they felt they had a grievance I would have an entirely different view in regard to it.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed ait eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six
o'clock we were dealing with subsection 10 of section 5.

Mr. Chairman, I intend
to move an amendment to this subsection, which deals with confidential evidence. I submit that such a provision is entirely without precedent in legislation of this kind, and that it could be very largely dispensed with particularly in view of the explanation given by the Prime Minister in regard to the way in which the board will function.
As was pointed out just before recess, this subsection provides for a penalty on summary conviction of SI,000 or twelve months' imprisonment. That penalty is imposed upon not simply the members of the board, its offi-

Tariff Board
cials, or those who are present and whose duty it-is to refrain from making public any matter subject to confidence, but as the subsection is drafted it imposes the penalty upon anyone who may happen to have information and who parts with it in such a way as to make it available for the use of any business competitor or rival of the person, firm or corporation submitting it. The general term "confidential" is not exact enough to be put into a statute which imposes such a penalty as this. The decision whether or not the information is confidential will rest with a court of summary jurisdiction, which may consist of two justices of the peace. Such a power put in the hands of a court of this nature is far in excess of that contained in any statute. The only one concerned is the competitor or rival of the person, firm or corporation before the board. If a person, firm or corporation were appearing before the board to ask for a duty there would be every likelihood that their competitors and rivals would be there as well, asking for a duty in connection with the same commodity. It seems to me that the competitor or rival is the very one who would have to know all the facts. He would be before the board assisting in the presentation of the facts, and I fail to see what the draftsman of this section had in mind when he restricted "confidential information" to the sort of information which might get to a competitor or rival.
No information should be confidential in the sense that it should be kept out of the report of the board and thus withheld from parliament unless it be information which would be considered confidential in a court of record. Information as to costs is not confidential. Such information must be before this House of Commons in order that it may determine whether the industry in connection with which duties are to be imposed or increased is entitled to that duty or is earning sufficient to enable it to carry on without the protection such a duty would afford. Costs of production cannot be considered as confidential, and if my right hon. friend has that in mind I submit that he would be depriving parliament of one of the important elements in connection with tariff schedules. However, I do not think my right hon. friend has that in mind, because he excepts any information brought out at a hearing of the board when the board is taking the place of the exchequer court or other courts provided for in the Customs Tariff Act, that is. a proceeding against any person, firm or combination of persons or firms for conspiracy in connection with the nrice of goods 22110-2251
or in connection with anything having to do with the exploitation of the consumer.
If this is to be a court of record, the rules which govern such courts should apply. The proceedings must be open to the public, except in two cases, with which my right hon. friend is familiar. First, the proceedings are not open where it would be against public .morals to make them public, and second, where a trade or secret process is involved, the very object of having a trade or secret process would be defeated if the person possessing it were forced to put in upon the public record. It is a well known principle of law that the administration of justice cannot be made the instrument or vehicle for defeating justice, and that would happen if a person were forced to make public a trade secret. I submit that this is the only class of evidence which should be considered as confidential. This rule applies in the Australian act and is contained in the regulations in connection with the United States tariff board; in those cases everything else is made public, and I submit the same rule should apply here.
From what my right hon. friend has said it would appear there is to be no prejudice to anyone appearing before the board. The board will conduct the examinations and it will be tender and gentle enough to see that no one is forced to give any information which might be prejudicial in the sense that it would be disclosing information advantageous to his competitors. The whole thing is in the hands of the board. In the first place the minister directs or requests the board, and then the board itself conducts the examination so that there need be no fear on the part of anybody that they will be forced to disclose something that will be to their detriment in connection with any competitor. The amendment which I propose will ensure to the man who has a trade or secret process the same protection that he has in a court of record; that is to say, he will not be forced to give away information with regard to that trade or secret process. But I want to go one step further. If he is willing, in connection with the inquiry, to give particulars of his trade or secret process, waiving the privilege which otherwise would be accorded him, then the court for this purpose should be cleared, the public excluded for the time being in order that information with regard to trade or secret processes might not be made a matter of general knowledge. But it must be remembered that the owner of the trade or secret process has the matter in his own hands; he may not waive the right or privi-

Tariff Board
lege and he may not be forced to give evidence. Therefore I desire to move, seconded by the hon. member for Hants-Kings, to amend section 5 by striking out subsection 10 thereof and substituting therefor the following:
(10) (a) Nothing in this act shall make it compulsory for a witness to disclose to the board any trade or secret process of manurac-tore.	.
(b) In case any witness is willing to waive the protection of clause (a) of this subsection the board may exclude the public from any hearing while the evidence of such witness respecting such trade or secret process is being given.

I hope it will not be thought that because I have not risen before I have not had occasion to object strenuously to some of the arguments put forward on the other side. This amendment indicates to me-and I say this with charity-that there is an attempt on the part of some hon. members, forgetful of the law as it stands, to offer as much opposition as possible to the passage of this bill. I am sorry to make a statement of that kind in the presence of the hon. gentleman who spoke last, but he knows as well as I or any other hon. member that no one in business can expect that the conduct of his affairs, the way he gains an advantage, if he gains one, shall be spread before his competitors. There is no question on that score, and so far as legislation on this point is concerned, it has been on the statute books for a long period of time. It passed the revision before the last one, but I have not had opportunity to look the matter up. My hon. friend knows, because we have had it mentioned before, that it is against the statute law of this country for the Department of Customs to show any invoice to anyone, no matter who he may be, unless under a subpoena or an order of the court.
What has that to do with this?

If my hon. friend does not understand, I think I can very soon make my point clear to him. If this amendment were to receive the sanction of this house, what would it mean? It would mean that except in the case of a trade secret or secret process, everything would be public. The inference would be, if this subsection were deleted and replaced by my hon. friend's suggested amendment, that invoices-this illustration just occurred to me because it was referred to last night-would then be the property of the public and if brought in evidence before the tariff board would be open

to the public. How ridiculous that would be! The customs branch of the Department of National Revenue during the administration of the previous Liberal government, prior to that under the adminstration of a Conservative government, if you call it such, and now under the administration of a Conservative government, has gained the confidence of the public. When we ask for information and expect to get it, they know it comes to us and to us alone. It is a splendid thing when the business of this country is carried on honestly and efficiently, and yet when every man in business knows no one can take advantage of him by using information given to the customs; otherwise all kinds of unfair competition would be set on foot.
What about the collection of income tax, if I may refer to it? The same thing might arise in connection with an investigation under this very clause that we have before us now. The income tax branch under both the former government and the present administration has maintained secrecy. There is a penalty for divulging information, and I believe this country collects hundreds of thousands of dollars because it is known that information can be given to the Department of National Revenue without any fear of its leaking out. If it does leak out, very drastic measures should be taken to deal with such a situation, and therefore there are penalties similar to those in this bill. I think the only thing I have to do to show the absolute futility of an amendment of this kind is to put it to any hon. member who is in business to say whether or not he would prefer, in the conduct of his business, that what he reveals and what he must reveal to the crown should be made known to his competitors. I know of no line of business, even in the professions, where one is compelled, or where it is thought to be fair dealing, to give, to competitors information in regard to transactions in connection with private business. The amendment goes a certain distance, but it does not go far enough. It would strike at section 182 of the Customs Act; it would strike at the provision of the Income Tax Act which says that the business of any man shall be confidential as long as he is within the law and does not seek to step outside it. I ask that this one-leigged amendment, which does not go far enough, be defeated, and that the section of the bill, which goes further should be adopted.

Following the example of my hon. friend, I shall endeavour to be charitable too. If he had read the section he would not have indulged in the worrisome

Tariff Board
portrayal of the difficulties of the manufacturer as he feared they would be found as the result of this amendment. May I point out that this amendment has not a solitary thing to do with the Income Tax Act; it has not a solitary thing to do with the Customs Act. It leaves them exactly as they were before. If my hon. friend had read the section, as he has not-and that is why I am charitable

he would know that. I will read the amendment for my hon. friend again.
I have read the section and the amendment, and this is later legislation than the Customs Act.
Then I shall have to withdraw my expression that I shall endeavour to be charitable.
I am not asking for charity.

Nor am I. This amendment says:
Nothing in this act shall make it compulsory for a witness to disclose to the board any trade or secret process of manufacture.
This amendment and this act simply mean that if someone is asking for duties in order, to use the expression we have heard so often in this house, that the cost of production in this country may be equalized with the cost of production somewhere else, he shall have to tell his costs of production. That information will have to be put on the record and be available not only to the board but to this house when the tariff schedules are brought down. There is nothing unusual about that. It has been in this country ever since it was a country. Manufacturers and those who have been asking for duties have always been expected to give their costs; otherwise a case could not be made. Does my hon. friend think we should act blindly in connection with these matters, that we should not know what the costs are when we are asked to impose duties that will equalize the cost of production? I submit that the term "ridiculous" which my hon. friend used is properly applicable to that proposition, if that is the proposition he is making. Ail that is being done here is to provide that when a man comes before the tariff board, which is a fact finding board, to which is referred this question of the equalization of the cost of production, to which is referred the question of how much of an increase of duty is to be given in order that the cost of production may be equalized-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not "is to be given."

The board which will
recommend how much of an increase of duty-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not that either.

How much should be
given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not even that.
We have been over the section time and time again, and the house knows and the country knows what its meaning is.
The hon. member evidently does not understand it, or else he is misrepresenting it.

I have read it half a
dozen times, and I can read it again, but the house and the country understand it to mean what I said. This board is to make a finding of fact, is to say what, in their opinion, is the increase of duty that shall be allowed in order to equalize the costs of production. If we have understood anything, we have understood that. Before that is done, surely we must have information as to costs.
The board must.

I have pointed out once or twice that the competitor is probably in exactly the same box with the gentleman who is making the application, and I do not think there is any particular reason why a man should be protected against his competitor when they are both applying for the same thing. I submit that in a court, as the Minister of National Revenue well knows, these things are not confidential. Nowhere else are they confidential. Why should they be confidential before the board? Nobody is asking anybody to make an application against his will. The Finance minister first of all has to decide whether anjffiody shall be asked even a single question; he need not make a reference to the board at all; the board need not ask a single question if they do not want to, and they can prevent any questions being asked. Is there any more protection that could be thrown around people who are asking for an increase in the tariff schedules?
My right hon. friend missed altogether what I tried to say. In the Irish act and in the Australian act you will find exactly this same principle and nothing more. There is no protection against confidential information in those acts, except as to secret processes, and in the Irish act I believe there is no protection of any kind. In the United States,
Tariff Board

where there would be a good deal of competition, and where the argument which my hon. friend made a few moments ago might apply, the only protection in their act is that no information shall be divulged that refers to any trade or secret process.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is more than that.
Just read the section.

Section 335 of the United States Tariff Act provides:
It shall be unlawful for any member of the commission, or for any employee, agent, or clerk of the commission, or any other officer or employee of the United States, to divulge, or to make known in any manner whatever not provided for by law, to any person, the trade secrets or processes of any person, firm, copartnership, corporation, or association embraced in any examination or investigation conducted by the commission, or by order of the commission, or by order of any member thereof.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not the section
I am talking about.
It is what I am talking about.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not the section constituting the commission.

If there is any other section I wish my right hon. friend would refer me to it. It goes on:
Any offence against the provisions of this section shall be a misdemeanor and be punished by a fine not exceeding $1,000, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both, in the discretion of the court, and such offender shall also be dismissed from office or discharged from employment.
There is a provision which has to do only with trade secrets and only with the employees of the board. It does not go the length of saying that confidential information cannot be made available to the competitor of somebody who is applying for an increase in the tariff. Further than that, it does not suggest for one minute, as this bill does, that somebody else who has nothing whatever to do with the board shall be subjected to fine and imprisonment. With that assurance I submit to my hon. friend that the strong expressions he has used and the apprehensions he has in mind are not well founded.
The hon. gentleman's amendment precludes the board from obtaining this information from witnesses before them without their consent.
Certainly.

Personally I desire the board to be placed in a position to obtain all information which it may regard as relevant.

There should be no prohibition against the board obtaining any information that it regards as relevant and material to the inquiry it has in hand. The hon. gentleman reverses that and says, by this amendment, that hereafter a manufacturer or other witness before the board shall not be compelled to disclose the real facts with regard to his manufacturing processes or many other matters which enter into the cost of production.
Not many other matters; just that.

I know enough about manufacturing to know that a number of matters which are very relevant indeed would be precluded under this amendment. So far as I am concerned I certainly could not consent to this amendment. The very basis of the whole proposed enactment is that in making legitimate inquiries the board shall have all information, and if information is withheld it shall be in a position to compel its disclosure. The hon. gentleman's amendment would prevent that.

All that my hon. friend is saying is that my amendment goes further than he would go in protecting the manufacturer. I am sure that I did not expect that objection from the other side of the house. With all deference to my hon. friend the Secretary of State, this amendment does not deal with a whole lot of things to which my hon. friend has alluded. It deals with just one thing, that a man shall not be compelled to give his trade or secret processes to the board.

The difference between us is that under the bill as it stands the applicant is compelled to disclose to the board everything. He cannot hide behind some objection of his own that this or that or some other fact desired would disclose some secret process.

I have looked at this with some care, and I wish to assure my right hon. friend that the matter has been very fully considered. . This is one of the cases outside of the matter of morals of which I spoke a minute ago, and outside of some matters expressly provided for by statute concerning young persons where courts are quick to see to it that nobody is prejudiced who has to give evidence before them. The reason is that once a secret process is revealed and the details given, the very object of that secret process is entirely lost. I have moved my amendment in the form of the provision in that respect in the Australian act, but I have gone a step further and have sought to waive

Tariff Board
the privilege of that section where the witness is willing to give the information, in which case the public shall be excluded while the evidence respecting trade or secret process is being given.
Let me go one step further. Where the public is excluded from the court room, in other words where a trial before a court of justice is held in camera, my hon. friend knows as well as I do that it is contempt of court to discuss anything which takes place. In such a case the applicant before this board, or whatever he may be called, would be surrounded with protection in regard to trade or secret processes. I admit quite frankly that this section is intended only to make such proceedings confidential, but I cannot conceive of anything mentioned in this bill which should be regarded as confidential in view of the fact that it has to be acted upon in the forming of a tariff schedule.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The section read by the hon. gentleman was a section dealing with punishment for breach of the observance of confidential relationships.
Which section?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The section dealing with the punishment of those who disclose confidential information. I read from a report which I have not now before me, but which will be found at page 3186 of Hansard, setting forth what the United States tariff commission did on the 12th of March of this year. It was from their act that this section is framed. At that time I referred .to an application for a reduction of duty on edible gelatin, and these are the words of the report:
The costs of production of the single Nether-land concern for the calendar year 1929, were obtained directly from its books.
To guard against disclosure of the Netherlands company's costs, either directly or inferentially, from the average cost of the domestic product, the commission has omitted the detailed cost data from this report.
If such information had been included the commission would have been doing what should not be done, namely, disclosing to the world the nature of a business. It is not intended that that should be done, but it is intended that the board shall get every form of information which may be necessary to arrive at a proper conclusion. There are some members of this committee, as there are people in all countries, who regard it as a matter of profound satisfaction to be able to nose into other people's affairs. That is always so. In this instance it is provided that no limitation shall be placed upon the knowledge which the commission may secure. If the knowledge disclosed is of a confidential character, then that confidence must be respected, and that is the action which was taken by the American commission in pursuance of the powers conferred upon it. That is the only way in which business can be carried on.
The hon. gentleman refers to the circumstances in court where the nature of the trial is such that the proceedings are held in camera. It is perfectly true that courts are hedged around with the safeguards he has mentioned, but it is also true that similar precautions are taken with respect to bank accounts. The English statute has been copied. It is also true that in courts of justice in such circumstances as my hon. friend has mentioned, unless it be essentia! to proceed otherwise because of fraud or for some other reason, names required in evidence are merely written on slips of paper, and various other similar precautions are taken.
The purpose of this provision is that without restriction or limitation the information shall be given to the commission. That knowledge, however, shall not be disclosed, because it might represent years of toil and the profit therefrom might be destroyed not only by competitors but by others.

That is not met in the
bill, that is just the point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is met here.
I think not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not met here? I shall
read the section:
Should evidence or information which is in its nature confidential, relating to the business or affairs of any person, firm or corporation, be given or elicited in the course of any inquiry, the evidence or information shall not be made public in such a manner-
That contemplates the information being made public.
Yes, go on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -as to be available for the use of any business competitor or rival of the person, firm or corporation, respectively.

That is the only man
from whom he is protected. My right hon. friend said that others were included.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, this section also
protects against the disclosure of that evidence to others. That is what the punitive powers are for, just as they are in the American statute. This section combines three things:

Tariff Board
(a) it ensures the obtaining of complete information;- (b) it limits the publicity of such information, to the board, and (c) it punishes for publication to other than "the board. -

No, for publication to a
competitor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, the punishment is
to any person.

But the publication is to a competitor. I presume my right hon. friend thinks he has made his point and has come to a decision. But the question is whether or not information which is absolutely essential to determine whether or not a duty shall be granted and tariff protection thereby afforded is to be available to this house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The answer to that is
very simple. If the information is of a confidential character, it is to be retained in the minds of the commissioners and not referred to in the report, just as was done in the American report in the case of edible gelatin. Comparisons may be instituted, but the information in the minds of the commissioners may not be disclosed.

How could my hon. friend institute a comparison if he had not the facts? I do not understand that. We have tp determine now whether or not the house is to decide on the facts which are presented, but the information with regard to cost is left out. If the American commission say they withhold the information I will venture the opinion that the evidence was given to a congressional committee or someone having to do with tariff matters. My right hon. friend has not yet produced the section to which I thought he was going to refer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My books are in the east block, but I read from the report.
But the report did not suggest it was being done under the authority of the statute.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, that is what it was done under.

I think my right hon. friend's remarks with regard to people minding other people's business are quite gratuitous. .Every day before the courts facts concerning the business of private litigants are presented in connection with which remedies have to be applied; the courts must ascertain those facts in order to apply the remedy. There is no doubt whatever that when some one comes to this parliament seeking tariff protection or an increase of duties already in effect, parliament should have knowledge of the facts.

How that can be so if they state the facts to a commission and the commission in turn does not pass the information on to parliament so that a vote -may be taken in the matter is something I find it difficult to understand. My right hon. friend says he is protecting industry from disclosure, but the section provides only that the information so disclosed shall hot be available to a competitor, and he is the only man against whom protection is given. The competitor is just as much interested as the applicant is in getting the same treatment with regard to tariff.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment.	[DOT]
No, the committee is not yet ready for the question. No hon. member on this side of the house has any desire to nose into other people's business.
Oh, oh.

And when an applicant comes before the government or the tariff board and asks for a handout from the public treasury in the nature of high tariff, then his business is no longer private, but it is our business. We are here to guard the business of the public, and when the. public is asked to make a contribution to the business of .an individual, it is the public's business to learn something about the business of that individual.
My right hon. friend says that costs will be treated as confidential. The section of the bill contains the words "information which is in its nature confidential." We know from our experience this session that the government has treated as confidential a good many things which are not of a confidential nature, l or instance I placed a motion on the order paper asking for the production of certain papers which had passed between the government and certain oil refineries. That information was refused on the ground that it was of a confidential character. All I wanted to know was what the oil refineries had aske.d for, and I am informed by the government that such information is confidential. It seems that hon. members on this side of the house are not to know what was asked for. I have reason to believe, that information which was given to the government in no confidential manner is being treated as confidential and is being denied this house.
This section of the bill provides that if any information is given to the board of a confidential nature, and if anyone reveals that information to the public or to some one who would make it available for that man's competitor, he would be liable to imprisonment. I cited a case in the house not long ago where a

Tariff Board
certain manufacturer refused to give information to the board in regard to his production costs except in confidence. The other party before the board said:	"We can figure that
out ourselves, we can get the information otherwise, we do not need to get it from him." Under this subsection, if he had done that he would have made himself liable to imprisonment.
Mr, BENNETT:	No.

If a man reveals certain
information how are you to know the source of it? He might say, "I did not get it from the board, I worked it out myself." The minister under this act is attempting to set up a board which he hopes will enjoy the confidence of the people.
An lion. MEMBER: So it will.

I think I am safe in saying that the confidence the people will have in the board will be in proportion to the confidence that the board will have in the people. If the attitude, is taken that the public is not entitled to any information, that all that is expected of the public is that it shall pay the shot,-if the board should feel no more confidence than that in the public, then the first time that board makes a decision against what [DOT]is conceived to be the public interest' the board will be regarded as rotten. If the minister desires to inspire confidence in the board, he should at least show confidence in the public.

Does not the right hon.
Prime Minister think that the word "wilfully" should be inserted before the word "violates"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think it is
necessary in this case.

I have in mind a case where somebody before the board might think that evidence which came out in an inquiry was not in its nature confidential, and he might publish it in the firm belief that it was in the public interest, and yet under this subsection he might be prosecuted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
Those in favour of the amendment will please say "aye."
Aye.

Contrary-minded will please say
"no."

Under the law as it is to-day there is an appeal from the board of customs to the governor in council. The Secretary of State the other evening rather took issue with me on that score and said that the appeal was to the minister. May I read to him the section of the Customs Act that I had in mind?

I was speaking from

Whenever any difference arises or whenever any doubt exists as to whether any or what rate of duty is payable on any class of goods,
IMr. Ralston.]
and there is no previous decision upon the question by any competent tribunal binding throughout Canada, the Board of Customs may declare the rate of duty payable on the class of goods in question, or that such goods are exempt from duty, subject in each case to an appeal within sixty days from date of such declaration, by any person interested, to the governor in council, and any such declaration of the board of customs when approved by the minister after the expiration of sixty days from the date thereof, or any such declaration when made by any order in council upon appeal, shall have force and effect as if the same had been sanctioned by statute.
That is exactly what I had in mind at first, that it must be subject to the approval of the minister, and there was an appeal to the governor in council.
I understood my hon. friend to be emphasizing the appeal to the minister but denying the appeal to the governor in council.
The minister must approve, then the appeal is to the governor in council. That is what I had in mind. I will withdraw it if I am wrong.

My hon. friend would not intentionally say anything that was wrong, and I do not think for one minute that he did so in this instance. It is section 54 of the Customs Act that I was quoting. To-day, when there has been an appeal, the board of customs decides, and within sixty days the minister may approve its decision. speechtext:
First of all, section 3 of the Customs Act provides:
There shall be a board of customs, which shall consist of the commissioner of customs or any officer for the time being acting as such, who shall be the chairman of the board,
And so forth. Then subsection 2 says:
2. The board of customs shall have such powers and perform such duties as are assigned to it by any act of the parliament of Canada or by the governor in council.

Tariff Board
3. Three members of the board, of which one member shall be either the commissioner of customs, or the officer for the time being acting as commissioner of customs, shall form a quorum and be competent to transact the business of the board at any meeting thereof.
Section 54 of the Customs Act provides:
Whenever any difference arises or whenever any doubt exists as to whether any or what rate of duty is payable on any class of goods, and there is no previous decision upon the question by any competent tribunal, binding throughout Canada, the board of customs may declare the rate of duty payable on the class of goods in question .... subject in each case to an appeal within sixty days from date of such declaration, by any person interested, to the governor in council.
If no appeal is taken within the sixty days, the minister approves the decision of the board, and that becomes binding on all parties. If appeal is taken and there is a reversal of the view of the board of customs, that reversal is published in the Canada Gazette, and that is the end of it.
Sections 11, 12, 13 and 14 of this bill provide that on proclamation the powers and functions and duties of the customs board shall be assigned to and be transacted by the tariff board constituted by this act, and the board shall cause its decision in any case brought before it to be published in the Canada Gazette. The governor in council may make regulations as may be deemed necessary for carrying out the .provisions of part II of the bill. Under these provisions section 3 of the Customs Act would be repealed from and after the date of the proclamation. There would then be under the Customs Act no such thing as a board of customs; section 54 would also go along with it, and there would be no appeal to the governor in council. I promised the h'on. member for North Waterloo the other evening that I would look into that question. My view now is at variance with the view I first held, because the effect of these provisions is that when the proclamation is made section 3 of the Customs Act is repealed, and there is no such thing as the board of customs under the Customs Act, the tariff board taking its place.

That is most unfortunate. That is the whole point. My right hon. friend now say3 that whereas heretofore the right of appeal to the governor in council has been reserved to anyone who felt that with respect to rates of duty the board of customs had given a decision not in the interests of those he represented, under this bill that right is done away with. I think that is quite wrong.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
