Probably my right hon. friend will say as the Minister of National Revenue said the other day, that the minister has to approve. I think I can speak for all governments when I say that the Minister of National Revenue is very likely to take the same view as the customs board or any body substituted for it, whereas the cabinet, representative of all classes in the country of agriculture and every branch of trade and commerce, may take a very different view when a matter is under review before it. As my friend the ex-Minister of Justice reminds me, that has happened before. We can speak rather feelingly upon that point. The governor in council, having a wider interest to consider and a larger view to take, is more likely to take a different view from the Minister of National Revenue, who is so closely associated with his board of customs. If there is any doubt about that appeal to the governor in council remaining, I think the Prime Minister ought to hold this section and see to it that when this court passes on any matter that affects a rate of duty there shall remain for a period of sixty days the right of appeal to the cabinet as a whole before that decision has the effect of law.

As it now stands a body of civil servants make the decision with respect to interpretation of tariff items; and if the minister approves, after sixty days the decision becomes law. If on the other hand a person who does not agree with the finding of the commissioners sees fit to appeal to the gover-
nor in council, the governor in council may allow or disallow the appeal, as the case may be. Part II of this bill, as I said the other day, substitutes for the civil servants comprising the customs board, who are permanent officials of the department and necessarily have an interest in its administration, this tariff board, which is-I hope I am not offensive in saying this-a non-political body. speechtext: Disarmament Conference

(Miss Macphail) had advised me that on such a motion she proposed to make some observations, and I arranged with her accordingly. So I assume before you leave the chair she will make those observations.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, I want to speak very
briefly about the approaching world disarmament conference to be held in Geneva in February 1932. It is a conference long anticipated and hoped for, and I felt while the house was in session we should have some discussion upon it.
I think the importance of this disarmament conference can scarcely be exaggerated. Lord Robert Cecil, who has given such wonderful devotion to. the cause of disarmament, and is probably the greatest authority in the world on it, spoke of the conference as follows:
It is one of those crucial events in the history of the world that must either succeed or fail.
I feel that it is the most important thing that we have faced in a long time. If it fails, the faith of people in the sanctity of international agreements will be blasted; and I think it is not too much to say that the future of the League of Nations hangs upon the success of this conference.
At the close of the world war, the allies, as they were then called-our group of nations -disarmed Germany and her associates, and it was distinctly understood that having done that the allies would proceed to disarm themselves. There is no doubt about it that in the covenant of the league and in the peace treaty this was distinctly stated, and though now we have gone a long time past the signing of the treaty of Versailles and the setting up of the League of Nations, we have not moved on to do what we then said we would do. I will put on Hansard the preamble of the covenant of the league, because in it is pointed out clearly our international obligation in regard to disarmament, and if we have respect for treaty obligations we can do nothing but carry out the solemn promises we then made. This is the preamble:
The high contracting parties in order to promote international cooperation and to achieve international peace and security by the acceptance of obligations not to resort to war, by the prescription of open, just and honourable relations between nations, by the firm establishment of the understandings of international law as the actual rule of conduct among governments, and by the maintenance of justice and a scrupulous respect for all treaty obligations in the dealings of organized peoples with one another, agree to this covenant of the League of Nations.

Article 8 of the covenant lays down very clearly that the members of the league shall formulate disarmament plans. I will read the first paragraph:
The members of the league recognize that the maintenance of peace requires the reduction of national armaments to the lowest point consistent with national safety and the enforcement by common action of international obligations.
While I am not going to deal with the particular subject of increased armament; armaments to-day are greater than they were when this clause was written. It is also true that in part V of the peace treaty we sacredly promise, if we regard our promise as sacred, to disarm ourselves when we had disarmed our enemies. The opening clause of part V of the treaty of Versailles reads:
In order to render possible the initiation of a general limitation of the armaments of all nations, Germany undertakes strictly to observe the military, naval and air clauses. . . .
And those clauses follow. In June of 1919 Mr. Clemenceau gave the following assurance
to Germany:
The allied and associated powers wish to make clear that their requirements in regard to German armaments were not made solely with the object of rendering it impossible to resume her policy of military aggression. They are also the first step towards the reduction and limitation of armaments, which they seek to bring about as one of the most fruitful preventatives of war, and which it will be one of the first duties of the League of Nations to promote.
Then there is the Kellogg pact as well. I need not give the exact wording, but in that pact we say we will never again use war as an instrument of national policy, and surely that means we are going to disarm. By all those promises we have made by international agreement we solemnly promise again and again to disarm. Not only that, but the council, the assemblies and the different committees of the League of Nations have, from year to year since 1919, dealt with disarmament, but still we are more heavily armed throughout the world than we were at that time.
I am not going to take time to go into the rather long drawn out and discouraging work of the preparatory disarmament commission which was set up by the League of Nations in 1925, and on which were representatives of the United States, Turkey and Russia. That commission finally made its report last winter -December, 1930-and they are ready now to submit a draft convention to the world disarmament conference which, as I have said, will meet in Geneva in February of 1932.

Disarmament Conference
While we may not be as happy as we should like to be over the draft convention I think we may take the word of those who know most about it that the draft convention is such that any degree of disarmament can be written into it. Lord Robert Cecil, in commenting upon it, just at the conclusion of the deliberations of the commission, said:
The conclusion to be derived from these weeks of strenuous work is that disarmament is a perfectly practicable policy. The issue now passes from the hands of the commission to those of the public. Do they or do they not desire that this policy shall be adopted? It only remains for an enlightened public opinion to insist that this greatest of all reforms shall be carried out.
Right Hon. Arthur Henderson, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Great Britain, speaking of disarmament in Queen's Hall on February 9 of this year, said almost the same thing:
The figures will depend upon the public opinion of the world. At the disarmament conference the governments will do what the peoples want. If the peoples want disarmament, they can have it. If they will exert their will they can compel results.
It is certain that the public opinion of the world is ahead of the action that has been taken in regard to disarmament, and I think it is also ahead of the opinion of the governments of the world in that regard. Right Hon. Arthur Henderson expressed that thought, when he gave what is called the Burge lecture, printed by the Oxford Press, in these words:
I do not fear what the peoples will say and think about us if we can but reach a disarmament agreement. . . . My doubts, my fears, are these: That the peoples will not understand the chance that lies before them; that they will not grasp the opportunity they have been given to fulfil the purpose which they all desire; that they will not make the governments understand that their delegations to the conference cannot be too bold, that they cannot go too far to suit their nations.
There is no doubt at all that Great Britain is most anxious, as I think every other thinking nation is anxious, that there may be real results from * the conference to be held next February. Lord Robert Cecil says he would like to see a great many nations take a stand for a twenty-five per cent cut all round. I do not know enough about it to know whether that is enough to start, but I do feel that Lord Robert Cecil knows a great deal about it. However, we do know that if we can reduce by a substantial amount the expenditures of the world in armaments it will be a gain for everyone and we will have relatively as much security as we have now, even for those who depend upon armaments for security.
22110-226J
There are very many ways in which one could show how earnest the people of Great Britain are in connection with this subject. Next Saturday a great mass meeting on disarmament is being held in one of the great London halls, and that meeting is to be addressed by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, by Mr. Stanley Baldwin and by Mr. Lloyd George. So you see they are not making it a party question there, and they are not leaving it just to the rank and file of the people. The first meeting they had in connection with disarmament was addressed by Right Hon. Arthur Henderson, from whose words I quoted a moment ago. This is the second large London meeting, and it is to be addressed by the three great leaders in the British House of Commons. I feel they are doing more than we have done here, but surely we can do no less than to say clearly and publicly-and I think our leading men should be careful to say it publicly-that we want to do our share in bringing about disarmament. These speeches to be made next Saturday will be recorded on sound films, and we will see and hear these three gentlemen in our own theatres very shortly.
I shall take only a very short time, because I hope some other hon. member will want to say something in connection with this matter. Lord Robert Cecil has written a most timely article in Time and Tide of April 25, 1931. He goes on to outline the possibilities'of what might happen, and says that it will be a catastrophe if success does not come out of it. He says the conference might break up without reaching any agreement, which seems unlikely, but he goes on to say that when we think of 1914 we must remember that anything may happen. So he does not want to take any chances. In the second place, he says, the conference may result in a mere codification of armaments at their present level, and that means failure. He goes on to say that because of our treaty obligations-if we have respect for those obligations-there is absolutely no way out; we must disarm. We hear a great deal of talk about scraps of paper in this country, and many references to the fact that Germany did not respect her treaties. Up to the present we 'have not respected our treaties with her, and it is time we began doing in relation to disarmament. I do not want to quote a great deal from this article, because it would take too long, but supposing the conference does fail; only one thing can happen, and that is a race in armaments^
Disarmament Conference

In commenting upon this possibility Lord Cecil says:
It is, then, no exaggeration to say that the most probable political consequences of an unsuccessful disarmament conference next year are that Europe will fall into two armed forces, and that the competition in armaments will revive; competition not merely between individual states, but, what is far worse, between two powerful groups of states manoeuvring for superiority.
Then may I give just one last quotation from Lord Cecil, because I do feel that possibly no one has done as much as he. He said:
Succeed we must. The alternative is too sinister for any man or woman of good sense and good will to contemplate. And there is a way to- succeed. Let those who share the convictions which I have expressed refuse to be sidetrioked by expert objections about the technical ", alue of this particular form of armament or that, and concentrate upon the one form of reduction of armaments which the ordinary citizen can understand and which comes within the scope of every parliament. Let them demand a definite cut in the total military expenditure of the powers represented at the conference. I believe that it is perfectly reasonable and possible-with dogged perseverance-to achieve at the 1932 conference an allround reduction of 25 per cent in the military budgets of those countries which did not have reductions imposed upon them by the treaties. This would be a first step

but a considerable step-towards that international equality which all serious students of European affairs foresee and accept.
Should this conference not succeed it would not be possible to go on increasing armaments over the world and still! keep Germany and her allies disarmed to the degree imposed by the treaty. That would be neither possible nor right. If we are not going to keep our word then we should not bind- Germany to an agreement which she made on the understanding that we would .
I believe much is being done in Canada and throughout the [DOT]world at the present moment to arouse public opinion upon this question and focus that opinion upon the governments of the different countries. But all the good1 work of the people will come to naught if a delegation is sent to this conference which is not of the very highest calibre obtainable, not equipped to take part in a very difficult task. I think the Prime Minister and the government are serious on this subject and I feed sure they will want to send a delegation which will prove to be of real assistance an this work. In my opinion that delegation need not foe made up of members of the government, nor even of members of this House of Commons. The Prime Minister and the government may not agree with me, but that is my opinion. The Calibre of (Miss Maophsil.]
these delegates is very important. They need to be not only well equipped mentally but they should believe in disarmament iby international agreement and1 be able to see the necessity of immediate action. If this matter goes another ten years, it will be ten years too late. A delegation could be sent from Canada composed of people who have made a detailed study of this subject. I have in mind four eminent gentlemen,, whom I would like to name as the Canadian delegation. As this matter is not in any sense a party matter it would be much better if our delegation were not made up of members of one political party. I repeat, that would not matter so much, but the delegates should believe in disarmament by international agreement. They Aould not be military experts, because to send military experts would be the most futile thing to do.
I hope some other hon. member of the house will feel inclined to discuss this matter. We have talked a great deal about matters not so important, and I feel that as private individuals and as members of the house we should do everything we can to make this conference a success. On the power of the individual, I would like to quote some wise words of Sir Robert Borden, recently written:
Who are responsible for the world's future peace? Wh°.- if not you and I and every individual unit in each nation? The sum of individual influences constitutes the public opinion of the nation: the public opinion of each nation enters into that of the world which determines war or peace.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to associate myself with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), and to support the request she has made on behalf of this great cause of disarmament. It is indeed a happy coincidence that she has started this discussion during the very week when a meeting is being held in Albert Hall in London at which the three leaders of the great political parties in England are to speak. Speaking in this house on the resolution to approve the general act for the pacific settlement of international disputes, I called attention to that coming conference on disarmament, and tried to impress the house with the necessity of Canada's being prepared to do her share at that conference. I called attention to the fact that in Great Britain the various parties in the British House of Commons were represented on an imperial defence committee, to arrange the representation to the coming conference and prepare the case for Great Britain.
We are facing many important problems. Unemployment has been referred to in this

Disarmament Conference
house from the national viewpoint, but it is an international problem. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was kind enough to let me have the report of the International Labour Conference, and I find that the whole time of that conference was occupied in the discussion of international unemployment and the making of an effort not only to find the causes but to apply the remedies. The problems which will be discussed at the international disarmament conference are of the utmost importance. I believe that the attention of this house and of the people of Canada generally has been drawn to the importance of the convention, and if it is not successful I am afraid that the edifice of international peace erected during the past ten years will be shaken to its very foundation.
The great work of preparation has been commenced. The hon. member for Southeast Grey referred to the draft convention which has been accepted and which is to be submitted by the preparatory conference to the various countries concerned. Reaiding the draft convention I notice that the personnel suggested, and as to which limitations will be made, is to be military in character, including customs officials, police of all kinds, forest guards and so forth. The same applies in connection with the air forces. An attempt will be made to limit the number and the horse-power of aeroplanes to be used in times of war even though machines not complying with these limitations are being used for civil purposes. But perhaps the most important feature is the creation of a permanent disarmament body or commission which will see to it that, the various peoples live up to the agreement that will be reached and will submit to the League of Nations instances of any infractions that may take place. Viscount Robert Cecil was a member of that conference, is was Hugh Gibson, United States ambassador to Belgium, who generally represents the United States in international conferences, and Count Bemstorff, the German representative. Each one of them emphasized the necessity of arousing public opinion in the various countries to the importance of the conference. The representatives of the various countries, including the men and women who will represent Canada at the conference, will be in some way the custodians of peace for the Canadian people. They will work for the lives and happiness not only of the present generation, but of generations that are yet unborn. But Mr. Speaker, experts and delegates at conferences cannot save us in spite of ourselves. Public opinion must be behind the movement, the scheme and the conference. Peace after
all is to a large extent a process of education. There was a time when kings could make wars with mercenary soldiers, hired troops, but those times are now past. In this democratic world, war cannot be successfully waged without the support of an overwhelming public opinion in the countries engaged therein. A policy of peace is not only an expression of views; it is a state of mind. It is a condition which is created amongst the various masses and classes in a country. Words of peace are needed, but they must be backed by deeds of peace.
I was pleased the other day to read that Ihe American Legion had adopted a resolution in support of this disarmament conference and asked the United States representative to work for its success. They know what war means. I think Canadians generally should not and must not forget the pledges that were given to those who fought during the great war. "Never again" was the rallying cry. The soldiers who fought the war were told that they were fighting to end all wars and that their sacrifices would be made for peace. They fought on account of those pledges, and those pledges must be redeemed even more than those concerning pensions or material indemnities or other things of that kind.
May I add that Canada is perhaps more interested than any other country in the world in the cause of universal peace. We are a new country; we have a great future; there is nothing to block our progress except wars, and we all know that wars in which we would be engaged cannot come on account of anything for which we would be responsible. We would not be the cause of any war, but we are interested in the maintenance of peace by other countries, because we know we would probably have to take part in war if it came. Canada has taken the leadership in the British Empire in accepting arbitration, which has now been accepted by all the members of the British commonwealth of nations. I believe Canada should also take the leadership in this question of general disarmament, and we ought to do our best in order that the men who represent us at the conference shall speak the mind of all Canadians and endeavour to establishd universal peace.
May I in conclusion read the words of a great soldier who is also a great statesman? I refer to General Smuts, who said last year:
Mankind has, as it were, at one bound and in the short space of ten years, jumped from the old order to the new, across a gulf which may yet prove to be the greatest divide in human history. . . . What has been done can never be undone. One epoch closes in the history of the world and another opens.
Disarmament Conference

I join with the hon. member for Southeast Grey in asking the government to see to it that Canada does her share at that conference so that as a result of its labours this great divide spoken of by General Smuts may be crossed. Let the government appoint suitable representatives, men who believe in peace-because if they think wars are necessary they cannot work for the great cause of peace. Let the government appoint representatives who have the backing of Canada, and we shall all try to support them, to give them a mandate which will be concurred in by the people in the various sections of the country, so that they may go to that conference and speak there the united mind of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BEYISKD EDITION
speechtext:
The development of democracy depends upon the maintenance of peace. War is destructive of all democratic forms of government. The declaration that this country desires to maintain peace is not sufficient. It is idle to think that permanent and lasting peace can come in our time merely by our making declarations and speeches. We have passed in the house and elsewhere resolutions in favour of peace; we have become parties to treaties of arbitration, and we have joined with other nations in declaring that so far as we are concerned war is renounced as an instrument of national policy. But all these renunciations, all these declarations, all these resolutions in favour of arbitration and peaceful settlement of dispute, either by recourse to law in world courts or other peaceful means, are useless except to the extent that they influence people's minds to think in terms of peace. If we are to have peace we must have it by cultivating and maintaining the spirit of peace, not the spirit of war. The warlike spirit is not consistent with the maintenance of peace, and the spirit of peace is an attitude of mind that comes from continuous education. It is therefore useful that we should from time to time make declarations so that the youth of the country may see the glories of peace as distinguished from the heroic achievements of war.
No man who reads history, no one who is familiar with the growth of civilization and with the heroic achievements of men who have given their lives on battlefields in every part of the world for high principles and great causes, can fail to realize that their example has inspired generations in days gone by and will continue to inspire noble achievements that are consistent with the courage and enterprise of our races. But in this age we realize

that war on any scale is destructive not only of the nations that engage in it but of the world at large. There can be no war of any importance now that doe3 not become general in its effects and influences. There can be no war in these days of scientific achievement in the use of poisonous gases, artillery, tanks and aerial warfare that is not fatal to the very development of civilization itself. We now realize that far from being a virtue war is the negation of all virtues and is destructive of the world's civilization. But in the face of all that has been said, as illustrating the point I desire to make, it will be found that to-day amongst the European nations there are many men under arms; equipment is being provided for war; men are talking in terms of the next great conflict, as though we had not been at the world's Gethsemane.
How are we to bring about the end we have in mind? We must do it, as I have said, by creating the will to peace, which comes from continuous educational effort. I said on one occasion in this city that we were paying a tribute to a great man for what he had done for the cause of peace. It is idle to think that we can ever achieve our end unless we destroy the means by which these wrongs are wrought, and that means disarmament, but disarmament, as was pointed out the other day by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, cannot be a one-sided thing. Hence it is that the conference to which the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) has referred becomes a matter of transcendent importance to the world at large. It is no longer a question of this nation or that. It is a question of the world itself. It is a question of the maintenance of our institutions, the maintenance of the life of our civilization. If this committee believes, and the public believe, as I am inclined to think they do, that peace can be brought about only by disarmament, it follows that disarmament must be achieved as soon as possible. But a one-sided disarmament is not possible. How is it possible to think in terms of disarmament if one nation has a million soldiers under aims and another has none? How is it possible to have disarmament when one country is in a position to ignite in a second a great conflagration, while another country will be destroyed by that very conflagration? No prairie fire of which we have ever heard could spread like the conflagration of military operations in communities divided only by imaginary lines. That being so, disarmament must be a worldwide state of mind.

New Westminster Penitentiary
This country in the northern half of this continent, this young democracy with its ten millions of people, freed from the horrors of all probability of war within its borders, its shores protected by the application of doctrines of an international character, has very little to disarm. I doubt if a disarmament conference could indicate any point at which we could disarm; for a police force is essential if peace is to be maintained and law and order preserved. The police force must be adequate to the task that is thrust upon it, namely, the preservation of law and order and the security of life and property. These things can be achieved only by an adequate and a disciplined and controlled police force. I do not think it can be said that either now or at any other time since the war we have had in this country more than an adequate police force for the maintenance of law and order and the security of life and property.
If all this be true, the extent to which Canadians can make a real contribution to the cause of disarmament is of course measured by the influence which they may exercise at any international gathering. The extent to which that influence becomes potent is not wholly measured by the number of muskets that it is possible for a country to create and maintain.

I say that unfortunately
the influence of countries has frequently been measured in that way. I am satisfied that this country, this new democracy, may exercise a real and a potent influence in international councils for the cause of peace. I pointed out this afternoon, as I frequently have in the past, and as I have heard my right hon. friend opposite and the hon. member who has just spoken frequently point out, that this country in international councils exercises an influence and an authority far beyond the extent of its population, its area or its material resources. It does that because it is itself a striking example of how peace may be maintained within one's own borders amongst people having their origins in different races, the one settled originally on the banks of the St. Lawrence, and the other on the shores of Massachusetts; and yet they have been able to fuse into one common sentiment their love of peace and their desire for the growth of democratic institutions. To the extent that our influence has brought peace and prosperity at home among men and women of divers races and creeds and of divers orders in life, to that extent it has increased from day to
day amongst the peoples of the world in international councils. The gentleman whom we honoured to-day as president of the League of Nations, coming from Canada in the early history of that organization, has been a potent factor in stimulating public interest in the movement for world peace and in bringing the name of Canada to the forefront amongst those communities whose influence has always been on the side of organized peace. That I think is common ground with us all.
I can only say this to the hon. member for Southeast Grey: That in so far as it may be possible, having regard to the time of year at which this conference is held, this country will worthily discharge every obligation that rests upon it in that regard, and I trust that the representations we will offer will not be unworthy of the great traditions of Canada in her struggle to maintain peace, in her belief in peaceful methods for the settlement of disputes, in her conviction that by recourse to judicial and arbitral methods the differences of peoples having been settled, the differences of nations may also be concluded. With that hope and that inspiration and that conviction this government, when the conference is held, will do its duty by the Canadian people.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house for a few minutes while I bring to its attention a matter of great importance to the constituency which I have the honour to represent.
I have telegrams and different communications here from New Westminster to-day to the effect that an investigation is to be held into affairs in connection with the penitentiary at New Westminster, principally with respect to some dismissals that occurred in 1928, when Inspector Jackson, now in charge of Kingston penitentiary, was temporarily in charge of the penitentiary at New Westminster. I am informed that the dismissals of two men in particular form the basis of this investigation. 1 would like to point out that there have been other dismissals, seven I believe, and those seven dismissals took place during the temporary charge of Inspector Jackson. These men had I believe asked for an inquiry, which had not been granted. I had not the honour to represent the New Westminster constituency in this house at the time these dismissals took place, or I would have pressed for an inquiry at that time. These men had given valuable service ranging from ten to over seventeen yearn, and were dismissed because at the time

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
the regulations governing the penitentiary were, to use that word, violated by those higher up. They were refused an inquiry at that time. I am going to ask the minister now if he will be kind enough to tell me whether an inquiry wild be held, and if so I should like such an inquiry to be of the fullest nature possible.
There is a further injustice concerning which many of the men are afraid to speak, namely that of long hours. Those men are working eleven hours at a stretch and are afraid to complain lest their complaints lead to dismissals. If an inquiry is to take place I should like an investigation to be conducted concerning the hours worked. I think however the injustice done to those men who have lost from $1,000 to $2,000 and were unjustly dismissed after serving from ten to twenty years should call for the fullest possible inquiry. I should like the government to be kind enough to make a statement regarding the matter.

If it is my right hon. friend's intention to consider the cus-

toms tariff resolutions I should like to say a few words now; probably it will save some time later'. My remarks will be directed to the views entertained by hon. members on this side of the house in regard to the consideration at this time of the proposed extensive changes in the customs tariff. On behalf of the opposition I should like to protest most strenuously upon being asked at this stage of the session to consider the vast changes proposed by the budget in the customs tariff of Canada. I take no exception to the government bringing in any changes it wishes to make in the tariff but I do submit in the public interest, unless those changes be other than nominal, or very limited in character, they should not have been brought in at this session of parliament, which was so late in meeting, and where there was no possibility of adequate discussion taking place until midsummer.
My right hon. friend has frequently stated that this is his first year in office. From the point of view of the general public I believe he has made the very serious mistake of trying to do in one year more than other ministries have sought to do not only in the life-time of one parliament 'but in that of several parliaments. He has not been satisfied with making changes in the tariff in a manner which he could himself explain, but he has sought to alter the complete tariff schedules of the country in a way which absolutely defies comprehension. If hon. members wish to applaud that statement I wish they would do so; however, that is the fact. Regarding the special session as part of the present one, the Prime Minister has sought in his first year in office to alter at least two-thirds-I think I am right when I say two-thirds-of the total tariff items of this country.

speechtext:
He is seeking
to alter half the customs tariff items at a session of parliament which comes within his first year of office, and to make those extensive changes in a way which renders it wholly impossible for the House of Commons adequately to discuss them or for that matter, to

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
discuss them at all. That is the exception I take to the action of my right hon. friend at this session and at the special session.
Hon. members on this side of the house feel that at the special session he should not have introduced any tariff changes. At the special session he had no mandate to revise the tariff, but he 'took advantage of the fact that an Imperial conference was being held in London to end discussion in a manner which to all intents and purposes amounted to closure, and as a result the tariff changes then proposed were scarcely discussed at all. He promised at that time that we should have ample opportunity at this session to consider the effect of the changes then put into effect, but that opportunity has not yet come, although we have reached the 8th day of July. We have not yet had an opportunity to consider any of the changes involved in the resolutions which at the moment are before the committee. I have no doubt my right hon. friend will say that we have been discussing the tariff bill and one or two other measures, but such comment would be entirely beside the point. My right hon. friend has the direction of the business of government, and had he wished to be fair to the interests concerned and to the people of Canada at large he would have done one of two things: either brought down his budget early in the session and afforded ample opportunity for discussion throughout the early weeks of the session, or waited until next year. Had he taken the latter course he would have had plenty of time to prepare his tariff changes and submit them at the beginning of a new session. Obviously in mid-summer, having regard to conditions prevailing in the country and to the temperature of this chamber, it will not be possible for hon. members to devote any considerable length of time to an intelligent discussion of the proposed changes.
First of all, if my right hon. friend intended to make such extensive changes he should have called the session at an earlier day; secondly, he should 'have brought down his budget earlier in the session, and thirdly, he should have given us a chance to discuss these resolutions at a time much earlier than the present. That is the first protest which I wish to make most emphatically.
I desire next to protest with equal emphasis at my right hon. friend asking this parliament to make extensive tariff changes without any preliminary investigation whatever with respect to their significance. This action on his part constitutes a departure from the. practice in Canada for yeans past under either Liberal
or Conservative administrations. For many years where a government contemplated other than nominal changes the ministry of the day appointed a committee of the cabinet to go through the country and conduct what were known as tariff hearings. Interested parties were allowed to appear before the ministers and make their representations with respect to what were considered by them to be necessary changes, and those opposed to such changes were given an opportunity to present their side of the question. In other words before any important changes in tariff schedules were made all parties were heard by a committee of the cabinet of the day. It was found that to send a committee of cabinet ministers through the country was not the most satisfactory way of dealing with the situation, and in the day of Sir Robert Borden, the then Minister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, announced to the house that a tariff commission would be appointed for ithe purpose of hearing representations as to increases or decreases in tariff, to give all parties interested an opportunity of being heard before- not after-the changes were made. That board was not. created formally by Sir Thomas White, the then Minister of Finance, he giving as an excuse that matters were running along so satisfactorily at the time that there was no necessity for any tariff changes of a material character, and hence no need for haste in the appointment of the board. The war intervened, and of course that was another reason why the board then proposed was not appointed.
When the Liberal administration came into office in 1921 a few changes were made in the first few years. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice. (Mr. Lapointe) reminds me that after Sir Robert Borden had resigned and Mr. Meighen was at the head of affairs, Sir Henry Drayton, as Minister of Finance, went through the country holding tariff hearings, with a view to the revisions that the government proposed to make later on. Every person was entitled to appear before him, and those who had opposing views were invited to express them. Then Mr. Fielding became Minister of Finance. 1 need not remind hon. members of the wide experience that Mr. Fielding had as Minister of Finance, and what that experience was worth to Canada; nor need I remind my right hon. friend of the great care which Mr. Fielding exercised before he made a single tariff change to see to it that all the .parties who might be materially affected were given a hearing before himself personally or before officers of his department who were in immediate touch with him.

When far-reaching changes were, proposed, such as the changes in the tariff on the [implements of production and later with respect to motor vehicles and the like, the government of the day gave, the fullest opportunity to the parties affected by those changes to be heard, and their views were fully known to the ministry as a whole and through the ministry expressed to parliament before those changes in the tariff actually were made.
Later the government appointed an advisory tariff board for the purpose of hearing the representations of those likely to be affected by the proposed tariff changes. It was the policy of the government that when an application was received with respect to an increase or decrease of the tariff, or when the ministry had in mind, for reasons of policy, making changes in the tariff, to refer the matter in the first instance to the tariff board. Then, the tariff board announced its hearings, which were held in public, and the parties in interest were allowed to appear and make their representations. Subsequently the board made its report to the minister, so that he had before him the point of view of all parties before he came into the house to present his proposed tariff changes.
The so-called Dunning budget, which went further in the matter of tariff changes than any other changes proposed by the late government, was not the result of a few hours or a few weeks study; it was the result of careful investigation that had gone on for.a period of two or three years.
Mr. R\ ERSON: An election budget.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It was not an election budget at all. At the time the Dunning budget was being prepared the intention was that the government of the day would be represented at the Imperial conference and that the election would not take place until a year after that time. But circumstances alter cases, and it so happened that the election came, as hon. gentlemen know, somewhat sooner than otherwise would have been the case. But the tariff board had been considering very carefully for a period of between two and three years the changes that were subsequently embodied in the Dunning budget.
What is the position with respect to the tariff changes that the Minister of Finance is now asking the house to consider? None of these changes has been considered by anyone except the Prime Minister himself-even if he has given them consideration. I do not believe he has had time to give them consideration. They are the most drastic tariff changes that have ever been proposed in

parliament. Whether considered from the point of view of the number of articles that are being changed or in relation to the extent to which the tariff rates themselves are increased, I think my right hon. friend has, from the point of view of the business interests of the country, done the most extraordinary thing that has ever been done by any minister of the crown. He has suddenly launched upon parliament vast changes, affecting half of the tariff structure, with the result that there is not a manufacturer, there is not a consumer, there is not a workingman who has any real sense of security at the moment with respect to the position of industry in this country. He has been making changes in such a precipitate manner that almost every few days he has had by order in council to cancel or amend those changes. In addition to that he has given to himself and his colleagues power to alter the tariff by order in council, so that what is done one day by parliament is altered the next day by the cabinet. I say that nothing of the kind has ever happened in the history of Canada before, and I cannot express too strongly the sense of injustice which I believe the country is labouring under through having its whole financial and commercial structure to some extent disarranged if not temporarily shattered, as a consequence of the violent changes in the tariff which my right hon. friend has made.
May I point out this further fact, that while under previous governments there was some opportunity for parties to be heard, the Prime Minister himself as a part of his own method of dealing with these matters has swept away entirely any possible consideration in advance of the changes he is proposing, vast as they are. It must be recalled that even the changes proposed in the resolutions we are considering have already been made and that the new rates of duty promised by them have been in force for some time. The Prime Minister abolished entirely the tariff board that was in existence when he came into office.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

My right hon. friend says, ''hear, hear." But, as I pointed out the other day, if he wanted any kind of investigation even by his own officers, there was a vacancy in the chairmanship of the board and he could have retired the other two members, and reconstituted the board to suit himself. To that board he might have referred the changes he was about to make, and the board might have advertised the fact that certain matters of the tariff were under consideration and given parties materially

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
affected an opportunity to be heard. But my right hon. friend did not do that. He swept the board out of existence, substituting nothing for it. He did not even give his own colleagues an opportunity of considering what he was doing, but by a stroke of the pen he gave instructions as to how the tariff was to be increased and changed, and then, presented it to parliament to be enacted within two weeks. That was at the special session last September.
This session he brings in a bill which he calls a bill to create a tariff board, but he takes care to see that all these tariff changes now being proposed, which go to make up half the total tariff, are made before that board is called into existence. So the effect of these changes is not going to be known at all until it is felt in the actual operation of the tariff itself.
May I say this to hon. members who think this kind of thing is helping the manufacturer, that in manufacturing one man's finished product is another man's raw material, and if you are going to permit tariff changes to be made in manufactured articles without any investigation in the first instance, you are operating in the dark as to the effect on manufacturing generally throughout the country. I think already my right hon. friend has heard from a good many interests as to the effect his tariff is going to have on their own and other manufacturing interests as a result of lack of carefid and thoughtful consideration being given to changes before they were made.
But there is a point I must stress even more strongly in regard to the changes my right hon. friend is making to-day, and that is the effect of what he announced in this house to-day and which has become apparent to the country for the first time-that the tariff board he is now creating, the one we have been discussing for the last two or three days, is not to be a tariff board before which interests affected by these tariff changes are to be allowed to appear and be heard; it is a tariff board which in its operations will be confined just to those particular things which he himself refers to it. In other words, these changes are not only to be made in the manner they are now being made, without any preliminary investigation whatever, but after they have been made, no matter how aggrieved the parties may be, whether they be manufacturers, workmen, consumers, agriculturists-in a word, whether they be engaged in mining, lumbering, fishing and agriculture, or in any branches of the manufacturing industry, unless it suits the will, the wish, the caprice of my right hon. friend there can be no investigation whatever into the effects of
these tariff changes. That is entirely wrong, and I do not think it can be defended on any ground whatever. I want to protest in the strongest possible way against the tariff being changed in this ruthless fashion, and at the same time against the lack of opportunity for redress being afforded to the parties themselves once the changes are made.
I know what my right hon. friend has in mind; he has said, "I am going to have a tariff policy which will prevent any commodities coming into this country which can be produced or manufactured in Canada, and I am going to put my tariff up to such an extent as to make that effective."

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite say "hear, hear", so there is no dispute about it. That means, as far as international trade is concerned, that it is to be cut off completely so long as there is a possibility of anything being manufactured or produced in this country. I do not believe the people of Canada have any conception of what my right hon. friend is seeking to do. I have done him the justice all along of saying I thought he had in his own mind a pretty clear conception, but I doubted very much if his own followers had an idea of what he intends to do. He thinks his particular policy is going to work out for the good of the country. I have given him credit for sincerity in believing that making Canada into an economic unit will be of great service to the country. But before any such policy is put into farce there should be afforded to this parliament the most ample opportunity for debate and discussion. I am perfectly sure that if we had an opportunity to discuss this policy on its merits many hon. gentlemen opposite who to-day applaud the Prime Minister for what they believe he is doing in such heroic fashion would be the first to ask him to move a little more slowly.
May I say that the changes my right hon. friend is making to-day are revolutionary in character. I think I am right in saying that changes with respect to economic matters, whether they affect prices, wages or the development of industry, should be along the line of evolution rather than of revolution. You cannot rip and tear up an existing system in a day or in a year without bringing about very serious consequences.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF AMENDMENT
speechtext: You did it before.

speechtext:
I wish my
hon. friend would allow me to speak; I am trying to make a dispassionate appeal to the

committee. If my hon. friend had a little more experience in public life perhaps he would not be so rude. The country is entitled to know what the Prime Minister is seeking to do. I think his own followers are also entitled to know, but I say honestly that I do not believe they know even yet. I say this in no offensive way; what I am saying now is being said in the presence of the Prime Minister himself, and if it is untrue I hope when he replies he will make it perfectly clear that it is not correct.
I repeat, the policy of the Prime Minister is so to restrict trade that commodities from other countries will mot 'be permitted to come into Canada if they can be produced or manufactured here. That policy is based on a conviction in the mind of my right hon. friend that trade must take place only as the result of some absolute advantage in production which one country possesses to the exclusion of another. I believe he is entirely wrong. Trade is based on no such doctrine. Trade is based on the doctrine of relative advantage, arising out of comparative costs of production. Countries have certain special advantages over other countries in the matter of production, and they devote their capital and labour more exclusively to the things in which they have that advantage rather than to those other things in which they are not so fortunate. They bring into their country even some things which they could produce or manufacture but which they could not begin to produce or manufacture at the cost at which they can be produced elsewhere. To make a simple illustration, if an individual has $100,000 to invest he might invest it in something which has a natural advantage in his own country in the matter of production or manufacture, and he would as a consequence be more or less sure of a return on his money. On the other hand he might put that $100,000 into something that has no special advantage, and probably he would get a very small return or none at all. International trade is nothing more than the result of that kind of thing on a vast scale. Production and manufacturing in a nation is the result of investment going into those particular fields in which special advantages are possessed, so that when trade is carried on internationally and there is more produced in any country than can be consumed there, the surplus is sent abroad in exchange for surplus products of other countries and the things which cannot be produced in that particular country under the same natural advantage.
My right hon. friend's policy is depriving the country of all the great advantages that

come from extended international trade, and that despite the fact that for years past the policies of governments have been so tO' develop the naitional economic life of Canada as to make possible a vast international trade. Large expenditures have been made by this parliament on our railways and steamships, whereby travel and trade are expanded to all parts of the world. There has been a policy in the Department of Trade and Commerce under which agents are sent to different countries. Later there has been a development in the matter of opening legations to assist in the discussion of international problems, and so on. The whole development of communication between different parts of the empire has been with a view to expanding trade within the empire and beyond its borders. To-day we have the projected development of the St. Lawrence waterway, not in relation to a purely national trade confined to Canada alone but in relation to a great international trade with other countries.
My right hon. friend's policies are absolutely defeating the expansion of Canadian, trade, and bringing about a crippling and restriction of trade in a manner that will be most serious so far as the future development of the trade and industry of the country is concerned.
I see it is eleven o'clock. I should like to say a few words on this matter when we resume to-morrow.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
